sources.title: Rita Levi-Montalcini (Q185007) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-15): English label 'Rita Levi-Montalcini', description 'Italian neurologist (1909-2012)', Italian and Korean labels present, instance of human, born 22 April 1909 in Turin, died 30 December 2012, citizenship Italy, the Kingdom of Italy (to 1946) and the United States, employer Washington University in St. Louis, educated at the University of Turin; a name search returns only this person as a human (other hits are schools, an asteroid, a crater and a family-name page). Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute, press release for the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (awarded jointly to Stanley Cohen and Rita Levi-Montalcini 'for their discoveries of growth factors') -- CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the Assembly's account that nerve growth factor (NGF) and epidermal growth factor were the first of many growth-regulating signal substances to be discovered and characterized; that Levi-Montalcini, then in Viktor Hamburger's laboratory in St. Louis, showed in 1952 that mouse tumours transplanted to chick embryos induced growth of sensory and sympathetic nerves without direct contact and concluded that the tumour released a nerve growth-promoting factor; that she developed the culture bioassay for NGF (the ganglion 'halo'); that the biochemist Stanley Cohen joined the group in 1953, purified the active extract, found the unexpected snake-venom activity and the mouse salivary-gland source (1958) and made antibodies; that excess nerve cells are produced in development and only those reaching a target that makes NGF survive; and that all groups that later found new growth factors followed in the tracks of Levi-Montalcini and Cohen. Award-body citation, honouring in tone (its statement that she moved to St. Louis in the early 1950s conflicts with the 1947 arrival in other sources). Read in full.

Nobel Foundation, 'Rita Levi-Montalcini - Biographical' (the autobiographical essay she wrote at the time of the 1986 award, published in Les Prix Nobel 1986) -- SELF EVIDENCE: her own chronology (medicine at Turin, the home research unit in her bedroom from 1940 inspired by a 1934 paper by Hamburger, the move of the laboratory to a country cottage, Hamburger's invitation to St. Louis, professorships there to 1977, a research unit in Rome from 1962 and the directorship of the CNR Institute of Cell Biology 1969-1978). Used only for orientation and chronology and to check dates against other sources; never as sole support for any row or card. Its family, wartime and refugee-camp passages were not used, and its date for the racial manifesto (1936) conflicts with other sources (1938). Read in full.

Lasker Foundation, 'Growth factors - NGF and EGF' (1986 Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award to Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen: citation and narrative) -- award-body account that her initial observation of nerve fibres growing into tumour tissue led to studies concluding that a soluble substance released by the tumour caused the effect, that tumour tissue implanted in the egg membrane without contact still drove nerves into inappropriate organs, that she devised a simple in vitro assay still in use, that she pursued increasingly refined NGF studies in collaboration with Cohen and others, and that her work was done without techniques later investigators took for granted. Its wording credits her with finding the same substance in snake venom and mouse salivary glands, which the Nobel press release, Cohen and the PNAS profile attribute to Cohen. Honouring in tone (promotional adjectives not used). Read in full.

Diana Lutz, 'Obituary: Nobel Laureate Rita Levi-Montalcini', The Record, Washington University in St. Louis, 8 January 2013 -- university obituary: her 1947-1977 research at Washington University; the repeat of Hamburger's limb-bud experiments in her makeshift bedroom laboratory, where studying the nerve cells at more frequent intervals led her to a different conclusion (cells proliferate and then die for lack of a maintenance factor); the fertilised eggs bought from neighbouring farms; an early curriculum vitae in the university archives listing 1940-1945 as a private laboratory; Hamburger's invitation in 1946; the tumour-bearing mice flown to Rio de Janeiro; Cohen's snake-venom surprise and the 1959 antiserum; the little recognition the work received at first; colleagues' recollections (Dehner, Allen, Woolsey); and the controversy over the Nobel committee's exclusion of Hamburger. Institutional obituary with named colleagues, admiring in tone; its note that she became director of the Institute of Cell Biology in 1962 conflicts with her own date of 1969. Read in full.

Washington University in St. Louis, 'Remembering Rita Levi-Montalcini', The Source, 10 October 2013 -- announcement of a memorial gathering with colleagues' and a former student's recollections: that Hamburger invited her in 1946 so that they could reconcile their disparate findings, that she became a full professor in 1958 and then established a research centre in Rome, and a student's account of her as a demanding but fair teacher. Short institutional item, admiring in tone; only the invitation and the professorship were used. Read in full.

Bernard Becker Medical Library, Washington University School of Medicine, 'Rita Levi-Montalcini (b. 1909)', Missouri Women in the Health Sciences biographies (2004-2009) -- library biography: the bedroom laboratory equipment in Turin, Hamburger's interest in two of her articles in foreign journals, her acceptance in September 1947 of his invitation to collaborate, her time at Washington University, the laboratory she established at the Higher Institute of Health in Rome in the early 1960s and the CNR Laboratory of Cell Biology she established in 1969, and her honours. Institutional biography, admiring in tone; its dates for her associate professorship (1951) and for the end of her CNR directorship (1979) differ from her own account (1956 and 1978). Read in full.

Mo Costandi, 'Obituary: Rita Levi-Montalcini', The Guardian (Neurophilosophy), 1 January 2013 -- press obituary by a neuroscience writer (also reproduced by the Society for Neuroscience): her repetition of Hamburger's experiments in a bedroom laboratory with tools made from sewing needles and watchmaker's tweezers and her different reading of the results (survival of newborn cells), the Bueker tumour result Hamburger showed her, her method for quantifying the tumour effect, Cohen's snake-venom and salivary-gland work, the neurotrophic hypothesis, Cohen's remark that she worked at great intensity, her strict work schedule to the end of her life and a last paper in 2012. Independent obituary, admiring; its date for the start of the Cohen collaboration (1952) and its '25 years' for the isolation of NGF are not used. Her marital status, UN ambassadorship and Senate seat were not used. Read in full.

Alison Abbott, 'Nobel Laureate Rita Levi-Montalcini dies at 103', Nature news blog, 31 December 2012 -- journalist's short obituary: a makeshift bedroom laboratory, her single-minded devotion to the study of how nerves grow, the discovery of NGF carried out mostly in the United States, the research institute she created in Rome (opened in 2005) which, in the writer's judgement, did not become the legacy she hoped for because of inappropriate management, and a foundation for scientific education of women in Africa. Independent journalism with a critical note on the institute; her Senate seat and parliamentary activity were not used. Read in full.

Nature editorial, 'Self-inflicted damage', 20 January 2010 (with the correction of 27 January 2010) -- journal editorial on the European Brain Research Institute (EBRI) in Rome: the 2002 launch spearheaded by Levi-Montalcini, the institute's international board, and the editorial's account that in November 2009, as president, she began unilateral procedures to dismiss the board and have it replaced by a commissioner (the correction states that any appointment would be made by the local prefecture), that board members called this contrary to the by-laws, and that the editorial found her stated reasons unconvincing, and, separately, a dispute with one board member over alleged late payment of bills. An opinion piece by an independent journal, critical in tone; her side of the dispute and its outcome were not available in the sources read, so it is used only for the documented facts above and the editorial's inferences about motives or the effect of her age were not used. Read in full.

Nicholette Zeliadt, 'Rita Levi-Montalcini: NGF, the prototypical growth factor', PNAS Classic Profile, 2013 (110:4873-4876) -- science-writer profile with named colleagues' comments (Cattaneo, Capsoni, Manca, Calissano, Chao, Snyder, Mobley): the bedroom laboratory (microscope, makeshift incubator, surgical instruments forged from sewing needles), her silver-stain work and different reading of Hamburger's limb-removal data, the 1949 joint paper, her repetition of Bueker's tumour experiment and the chorioallantoic-membrane control, the 1952 trip to Rio de Janeiro with tumour-bearing mice to learn tissue culture, Cohen's snake-venom surprise and salivary-gland source, the 1960 antiserum experiments with Barbara Booker that answered doubts about NGF's physiological role, her late project at the EBRI (about 2007-2012), and its note that she founded the EBRI in 2002. Independent science-writer profile, admiring, with several details traceable to her autobiography; her health, family and early-life passages were not used. Read in full.

Stanley Cohen, 'Origins of growth factors: NGF and EGF', Journal of Biological Chemistry (Reflections), 2008 (283:33793-33797) -- the co-laureate's first-hand account of the NGF work as seen from the biochemist's side: that Hamburger and Levi-Montalcini sought a biochemist for the problem, that because each side knew little of the other's field they interacted but never argued, that she repeated Bueker's tumour experiment and found sensory and sympathetic fibres entering the tumour and reaching tissues they should not enter, that she placed the tumour on the chorioallantoic membrane to show a soluble diffusible agent, that she devised a hanging-drop culture assay, that she injected the purified venom protein into the yolk sac of chick embryos, and the antiserum experiments. First-hand colleague testimony (not her own), friendly in tone; the EGF half of the article was not used. Read in full for the NGF part.

L. Coutinho and H. A. G. Teive, 'Rita Levi-Montalcini: the neurologist who challenged fascism', Arquivos de Neuro-Psiquiatria, 2023 (81:95-98) -- scholarly biographical article: her training and career chronology, the Rio de Janeiro stay of September 1952 to January 1953 (permission from Carlos Chagas Filho, work in Hertha Meyer's laboratory because her own facilities lacked tissue-culture capacity, two sarcoma-bearing mice in her handbag, several negative results before the cultures responded), the initial scepticism towards NGF and the delayed recognition, and the 2002 co-founding of the EBRI with Pietro Calissano. Secondary historical article relying on her Nobel autobiography and other retellings, admiring in tone; its persecution framing and her political and social passages were not used. Read in full.

Accademia Nazionale delle Scienze detta dei XL, 'Rita Levi-Montalcini. A life with neurons' (note introducing Pietro Calissano's 2017 book) -- short academy note quoting the introduction by the neuroscientist who worked with her from 1965: that he saw her every day for more than four decades and that her personality was a mixture of intuitive skills and a total, almost monastic dedication to work. Institutional blurb quoting a close colleague, admiring; used only for that one characterisation. Read in full.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Rita Levi-Montalcini (1986).jpg' -- checked for the portrait's file, creator and licence: 'Rita Levi-Montalcini during a visit to Lund, Sweden, in 1986', date 12 December 1986, source University Library, Lund University (Alvin record 240038), author Kurt Hagblom, Firma Hagblom-Foto, restored by Adam Cuerden (a Commons and English Wikipedia featured picture, December 2025), licence tag PD-copyright holder (the copyright holder, Universitetsbiblioteket, Lunds universitet, released it into the public domain), original JPEG 2517 x 3796 pixels. Not used for any scoring.

Lund University Library, Alvin record alvin-record:240038, 'Nobelprisdam besöker Lund - Rita Levi-Montalcini (medicin/fysiologi)' -- the institution's own record of the press photograph (read through the Internet Archive capture of 13 January 2026 of the record's image-viewer page, because the live Alvin site serves a bot-check page to scripts and that check was not bypassed): photographer 'Firma Hagblom-Foto', origin Lund, Sweden, 1986-12-12, press-photo assignment for the newspaper Arbetet, negative from the Hagblom-Foto collection (about 1,200,000 negatives, donation 2012), 'Licensing of the work: Public Domain Mark (No Known Copyright)', and Alvin's general statement that all digitized materials in Alvin may be downloaded and used freely. No conflicting rights notice was found. Not used for any scoring.

persistence.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_nobel_press, src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_coutinho, src_levimontalcini_washu_obit, src_levimontalcini_guardian | 1952-2012 | award-body citation + science-writer profile with colleagues' comments + scholarly biography + university obituary + press obituary] The Nobel Assembly describes her study of NGF in the development and later function of the nervous system as a lifelong dedication; the PNAS profile reports that when injecting tumour extracts into embryos failed to reproduce the tumour's effect she moved the work into tissue culture, and Coutinho and Teive record that her 1952-53 stay in Rio de Janeiro gave several negative results before the cultures responded to the sarcomas; PNAS adds that, because NGF's unusual sources (tumours, venom, salivary glands) left many scientists doubting its physiological relevance, she and Barbara Booker tested it in newborn mice with an NGF antiserum, and the WashU obituary says that by 1959 the antiserum had been developed yet the work still drew little recognition; the Guardian says she kept a strict and rigorous work schedule to the end of her life with a last paper in 2012, and the PNAS profile has EBRI colleagues describing her coming to the laboratory almost every day and starting a new NGF project around 2007. Several independent descriptions across six decades with specific episodes, but the sources are admiring, the Rio details trace partly to her own recollections as relayed, and continuity of purpose is a recurring theme rather than a measured quantity, so documented at a moderately high confidence and held below the top band; the wartime home laboratory and its political circumstances are not used for this row (they are context, not scored). LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the behavioural account comes from tributes, obituaries and a science-writer profile that are broadly admiring, with the one critical source (Nature 2010) concerning governance rather than method; score and confidence lowered.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_washu_obit, src_levimontalcini_cohen_jbc, src_levimontalcini_nobel_press, src_levimontalcini_lasker | 1940s-1960 | science-writer profile + university obituary + co-laureate's account + award-body citation + award-body narrative] The PNAS profile says she examined chick embryos over a wide range of time intervals after limb removal and saw nerve cells multiply and then die, and the WashU obituary likewise says she studied the nerve cells at more frequent intervals than Hamburger and read the same operation differently; for the tumour work PNAS and Cohen both describe the control that placed the tumour on the chorioallantoic membrane, out of contact with the embryo's tissues, to show that a soluble factor was responsible, and Cohen adds that she injected the purified venom protein into the yolk sac as a further in vivo test; the Nobel Assembly credits her with the biological assay used to measure NGF (a graded halo of outgrowing fibres) and the Lasker Foundation describes a series of studies leading to the conclusion of a soluble substance; PNAS reports that she and Booker then tested NGF's function in newborn mice with an antiserum. Stepwise, control-based testing documented by an award body, a university, a science writer and her co-laureate, but the 1940s details rest largely on her own account as relayed, credit for individual steps is shared with Hamburger and Cohen, and the accounts are admiring, so documented at a moderate-to-high confidence. LEAD REVIEW CORRECTION (Roster50, before eligibility, downward only): the behavioural account comes from tributes, obituaries and a science-writer profile that are broadly admiring, with the one critical source (Nature 2010) concerning governance rather than method; score and confidence lowered.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_washu_obit, src_levimontalcini_guardian, src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_cohen_jbc, src_levimontalcini_lasker, src_levimontalcini_nobel_press | 1940s-1950s | university obituary + press obituary + science-writer profile + co-laureate's account + award-body narrative + award-body citation] Three independent accounts (WashU, the Guardian and PNAS) describe her reading Hamburger's limb-removal results differently: where he had concluded that the missing limb withheld a signal needed for nerve cells to form, she concluded that the cells formed and then died for lack of a factor needed to maintain them; Cohen contrasts the earlier grafting researcher Elmer Bueker, who took the tumour to be a favourable field for sensory fibres, with her conclusion that it released a soluble, diffusible agent; the Lasker Foundation calls her concept that cell growth is governed by soluble substances original, and the Nobel Assembly describes the NGF discovery as a skilled observer creating a concept out of apparent chaos. Limits: the WashU obituary reports controversy over the Nobel committee's exclusion of Hamburger and that two of his former colleagues argued that his observations and model underlay the later work, so credit for the original ideas is shared and this row concerns her interpretive choices, not sole authorship; the sources are admiring, so documented at a moderate confidence.

curiosity.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_cohen_jbc, src_levimontalcini_guardian, src_levimontalcini_coutinho, src_levimontalcini_nobel_press | 1947-2012 | science-writer profile with colleagues' comments + co-laureate's account + press obituary + scholarly biography + award-body citation] The Guardian says Hamburger showed her Bueker's result with grafted mouse tumours and that she investigated it, PNAS says that, intrigued, she repeated the experiment right away, and Cohen likewise says she decided to repeat it on arriving in St. Louis; Coutinho and Teive record that she asked to work in Hertha Meyer's laboratory in Rio de Janeiro because her own facilities could not support tissue culture; an EBRI postdoctoral colleague (Manca) says in PNAS that she was very curious about new technologies, techniques and everything the group did and came with a new idea almost every day, and her colleague Antonino Cattaneo says that around 2007 she kept re-examining her own old results from different angles and asked whether NGF might act earlier in development than she had found, which led to a new set of experiments; the Nobel Assembly describes the NGF discovery as a skilled observer building a concept from apparent chaos. Several specific episodes from the 1940s to 2012, but the late-career testimony comes from two EBRI colleagues, the early episodes partly rest on her own recollections as relayed, and the sources are admiring, so documented at a moderate confidence.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_cohen_jbc, src_levimontalcini_nobel_press | 1930s-2007 | science-writer profile with colleagues' comments + co-laureate's account + award-body citation] PNAS says that as a student she perfected the silver-staining method for nerve cells and made the tedious nerve-cell counts her early project required, that in the tumour experiments she noticed the nerve fibres entering the tumour did not make direct connections with its cells and that tissues far from the tumour were flooded with fibres unusually early, and that around 2007 she taught the EBRI group, which lacked chick-embryo experience, how to inject early embryos and what to look for under the microscope; Cohen separately says she found that both sympathetic and sensory fibres entered the tumour and reached tissues they should not have; the Nobel Assembly describes the discovery as the work of a skilled observer. Observational care documented in specific episodes by a science writer and her co-laureate, but the student-years details rest on her own account as relayed and the Assembly's statement is a brief general characterisation, so documented at a moderate confidence; the temporal-sampling evidence is carried by the analytical rigor row, not repeated here.

collaboration.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_nobel_press, src_levimontalcini_cohen_jbc, src_levimontalcini_lasker, src_levimontalcini_washu_obit, src_levimontalcini_washu_remembering, src_levimontalcini_becker, src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_accademia_xl | 1947-2012 | award-body citation + co-laureate's account + award-body narrative + university obituary + university news item + library biography + science-writer profile + academy note] The Nobel Assembly records that Cohen joined her group in 1953 and that the group followed up the unexpected snake-venom result together; Cohen himself writes that she and Hamburger, neither a biochemist, looked across the university for a biochemist and that, because each side knew little of the other's field, they interacted but never argued; the Lasker Foundation describes inspiring and extraordinarily fruitful collaborations with Cohen and other investigators; WashU and the Becker Library say Hamburger invited her to St. Louis after reading her papers so that the two could reconcile their differing findings, and PNAS lists their 1949 joint paper; PNAS adds that around 2007 she supervised the EBRI group's embryo injections and taught them what to look for, and the academy note quotes Calissano on seeing her every day for more than four decades. A sustained set of partnerships documented by her co-laureate, award bodies and institutions over six decades, but the sources are admiring, credit for particular steps is partly disputed (the Nobel committee's omission of Hamburger drew controversy per WashU), and the evidence is about scientific partnerships rather than day-to-day working relations, so documented at a moderate-to-high confidence.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_coutinho, src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_becker, src_levimontalcini_nature_editorial | 1952-2007 | scholarly biography + science-writer profile + library biography + journal editorial] Several separate instances of initiating work: Coutinho and Teive say she asked Carlos Chagas Filho for permission to work in Hertha Meyer's laboratory in Rio and travelled there in 1952; the Becker Library biography says she established a laboratory at the Higher Institute of Health in Rome in the early 1960s and the CNR Laboratory of Cell Biology in 1969; Nature's 2010 editorial says the 2002 launch of the EBRI was spearheaded by her and PNAS says she founded it; PNAS reports that around 2007 she asked a colleague for help starting a new project, proposed the antibody method for it and taught the group the embryo injections. A pattern across independent sources over five decades, but the first-hand material is partly her own recollection relayed by others, the late-career evidence rests on one colleague's account, and the founding instances overlap with the leadership row, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_levimontalcini_becker, src_levimontalcini_lasker, src_levimontalcini_nature_editorial, src_levimontalcini_nature_blog, src_levimontalcini_pnas, src_levimontalcini_coutinho | 1961-2010 | library biography + award-body narrative + journal editorial + journal blog obituary + science-writer profile + scholarly biography] The Becker Library biography says she established a laboratory at the Higher Institute of Health in Rome in the early 1960s and, from 1969, the CNR Laboratory of Cell Biology in Rome, which she directed until 1979 (the Lasker Foundation lists her at the CNR Institute of Cell Biology in 1986; her own Nobel biography gives the directorship as 1969-1978); Nature's 2010 editorial says the 2002 launch of the EBRI was spearheaded by her, PNAS says she founded it in 2002 and Coutinho and Teive say she co-founded it with Pietro Calissano. On the other side, the same editorial reports that as president in late 2009 she began unilateral procedures to dismiss the board of directors and replace it with a commissioner (its correction states that any appointment would be made by the local prefecture), that board members called this contrary to the by-laws, and that Nature found her stated reasons unconvincing, and Nature's 2012 obituary blog says inappropriate management kept the institute from becoming the legacy she hoped for. Repeated founding and leading of research institutions is documented, with one contested governance episode reported by Nature and board members; her side and the outcome were not available in the sources read, so no judgement is made on the merits, her motives or any effect of age, and the evidence supports a moderate score at a modest confidence with a dual-edged impact.

Four observers across different decades describe regular, intense work habits, but these are brief characterisations by admiring colleagues and journalists rather than a measured routine, and the evidence overlaps with the persistence row (which concerns continuing through setbacks and the NGF programme, not the daily schedule), so strong inference at a modest confidence.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT (2026-10-15, before deep research): QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities for Q185007 returned en label 'Rita Levi-Montalcini', description 'Italian neurologist (1909-2012)', Italian and Korean labels present (the Korean label and the Korean Wikipedia article title agree on 리타 레비몬탈치니), instance of human, born 1909-04-22 in Turin, died 2012-12-30, citizenship Italy, the Kingdom of Italy (to 1946) and the United States, employer Washington University in St. Louis; a wbsearchentities search on her name returned only this person as a human (the other hits are schools, an asteroid, a crater and a family-name page), so the lead's hint is the Italian neurologist and not another entity. REGION: southern_europe (valid id), a choice between origin and career recorded here: she was born and trained in Turin, worked at Washington University in St. Louis from 1947 to her retirement in 1977 (Nobel biography, Becker Library, WashU obituary), and from the 1960s divided her time with Rome, where she later led CNR laboratories and founded the EBRI; the repository's dominant convention for emigrant scientists is the region of origin (Enrico Fermi IT and US is southern_europe, the closest Italian precedent; also John von Neumann, Nikola Tesla, Freeman Dyson, Chandrasekhar, Zewail, Chien-Shiung Wu and Katalin Kariko), with Emilio Segre, Maria Goeppert Mayer and I. M. Pei as north_america exceptions; origin was chosen for consistency with Fermi, and it also matches her later base in Rome, while her US career is carried by nationalityCodes IT and US (US citizenship is taken from Wikidata, whose two references were not opened; her National Academy of Sciences membership appears in the Becker Library biography). Vocabulary ids (occupations biologist, medical_researcher and scientist, fields biology and natural_science, impact domains scientific and medical, tag nobel_laureate, archetype scientific_explorer) already exist and are used by other candidates (Jennifer Doudna, Katalin Kariko, Santiago Ramon y Cajal); the tag late_recognition was not applied because her honours accumulated from the 1960s onward (Becker Library biography), so recognition was gradual rather than late; era 20th_century as for other people born 1900-1925. DECEASED SUBJECT: only documented public professional conduct is scored. EXCLUDED: family and private life (her parents, twin sister, siblings, marital status, childhood, her father's views, clothing and scent anecdotes), health and the physical effects of age, her wartime flight, hiding and refugee-camp medical work, the racial laws and the persecution biography (the bedroom laboratory is used only as a work method and the political circumstances are named as context, never as the source of a trait; no personality is inferred from persecution, trauma or age), the Fidia and Cronassial allegations and any other allegations (not opened and not used), and the Pope-protocol anecdote (a single anecdote).
